reply:
No. The salt stops rainbow tables, but you're not accounting for the real threat: brute force.

The concrete cost of being wrong: when your password database leaks (they do), attackers crack weak passwords in hours on a GPU. MD5 is ~1000x faster than bcrypt per guess. That's the gap between "online cracking tool finishes in your lunch break" and "would take weeks even with hardware."

The pentester isn't being pedantic. They saw a database they can hash-spray against at scale. A unique salt per user doesn't change that—it just means the attacker can't reuse one cracking run across users. Each password still falls to billions of MD5 attempts per second.

"No practical preimage attack" is true but irrelevant. The threat isn't finding *a* preimage; it's trying millions of common passwords and variations until one matches *your* hash. Speed is the attacker's friend there.

What would change my mind: threat model that includes "password database stays secret forever" and "users only pick passwords with 10+ bits of entropy." That's not most organizations.

grade.note: Reply reaffirms slow-hash necessity, correctly distinguishing brute force from rainbow table/preimage concerns.
